sections.html:
Doña Ana County is in the south of New Mexico along the Texas and Mexico borders. It has more than 219,500 residents and includes the cities of Anthony, Las Cruces and Sunland Park, the Town of Mesilla and the Village of Hatch.

Las Cruces, the county seat, is the biggest city in southern New Mexico (111,385 people in 2020) and the hub of the Mesilla Valley, a farming area on the Rio Grande floodplain.

Sellers here may hold a Las Cruces city lot, an irrigated farm parcel or open desert acreage, all under one tax office. Each one is taxed at a rate built from the city, schools and special districts covering it.

Valuation is the Doña Ana County Assessor's job, and billing and collecting belong to the Doña Ana County Treasurer. The Assessor does not tax anything.

The state sets every taxing entity's rate, called the mill levy, through its Department of Finance and Administration. Cities, school districts and other bodies draw their share based on what they budget.

Multiply taxable value, less exemptions, by the mill rate. One-third of assessed value counts as taxable. Your own district's rate is posted on the Assessor's site.

Two payments make up the year. November 10 is the first-half due date, and December 10 is the last day before that half is delinquent. April 10 and May 10 play the same roles for the second half.

DateEvent
January 1Property valued; liens attach to delinquent real and personal property
January 10Deadline to file claims for refund in District Court
April 10Second installment comes due
May 10Second installment turns delinquent
June 10Delinquent notices mailed and notices of transfer to the state
July 1Treasurer transfers the delinquent roll to the state
October 1Treasurer receives the tax roll from the Assessor
November 1Bills mailed
November 10First installment comes due
December 10First installment turns delinquent

Delinquency charges begin on December 11.

Each month the balance sits unpaid, interest of 1% of the base tax is added, along with a 1% penalty that can build for up to five months, never below $5. A bounced check costs $25.

No law allows a county treasurer to waive penalty or interest, and nobody else can erase them once they accrue. A bill that never shows up does not excuse you, because the obligation to pay stands either way.

The consequences escalate over time:

  • Every June, the Treasurer mails a notice on any bill that is 30 or more days delinquent.
  • Delinquent taxes are transferred to the state's Property Tax Division on July 1.
  • Real property two years past its delinquency date can go to a state public auction.
  • With three or more prior years owing, the property is sold unless every year is paid in full before the sale.
  • Manufactured homes and personal property may be seized and sold after six months.

If you cannot pay everything, the state Property Tax Division may offer an installment agreement that halts a sale.

sections.h2: How to protest or reduce your bill
sections.html:
Send the County Assessor a valuation protest within 30 days of the date printed on the Notice of Value, typically in April. Miss that and your remaining path is paying everything by December 10, then asking District Court for a refund by January 10.

A pending protest does not suspend payment. Pay at least the tax on the undisputed value when the half comes due: December 10 and May 10. If a protest results in a corrected bill, it carries a new delinquency date and arrives at least 30 days before payment is due, without interest or penalty on the amended amount.

There is no homestead exemption in New Mexico. Relief comes in three forms:

  • Head of Family, for a resident whose primary residence it is. You apply once and it continues, one per household.
  • A veteran exemption, which requires a certificate from the state's veteran service commission, taken to the Assessor during the Notice of Value period.
  • A valuation freeze, available to owners who are 65 or older or disabled with modified gross income under $35,000. You apply three years running, and after that it holds for as long as you live in the home.

Check the current income limit with the Assessor first.

The January 1 owner of record answers for that year's tax. A lien remains on the property whoever owns it next. The Treasurer cites section 7-37-7 NMSA 1978 for this rule.

Prorating is not something the county does. If buyer and seller want to share the year, the sale contract and the title company's closing statement have to say so. If the property is mortgaged, make sure the lender has paid. The county does not mail an escrowed bill to the owner, though you can request one.

Special situations to watch:

  • Before a mobile home's title can transfer, or a moving permit issue, the Assessor must give a property tax release, and personal checks do not work for that payment.
  • Splitting or combining land requires all taxes paid, current year included, before the Treasurer issues a Certification of Taxes Paid.
  • A closed business still owes tax for the year if it operated on January 1.

Farm parcels, inherited land and years of back tax lead many owners to an as-is cash sale, where the tax is paid out of the sale money.

A workable order: get the Treasurer's payoff, check exemptions with the Assessor, and give both numbers to your closing agent. Bring your deed too. If you plan to split farm acreage, say so before you sign anything.

sections.h2: Preparing a Doña Ana County sale
sections.html:
Doña Ana sales usually go smoother when the tax picture is clear before the first showing. The steps below suit most owners.

  1. Request the Treasurer's balance for each year, not just this one. Older years are the ones that move a parcel toward the state list.
  2. Confirm with the Assessor that Head of Family or the veteran exemption is on the record, and note the Notice of Value date in case a protest is still possible.
  3. If the land is farm acreage or part of a larger tract, find out whether a split is planned, since the Treasurer certifies taxes paid only after everything owed is cleared.
  4. Give the closing agent your deed and the payoff numbers, and the year can be divided fairly between you and the buyer.
  5. With a lender escrow, verify that the lender actually paid. No escrowed bill is mailed to you unless you request it.

With no lender appraisal to wait on, a cash as-is closing is paced mainly by how quickly the tax balance and title clear.

faqs.q: When are Doña Ana County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due November 10, and it turns delinquent once December 10 passes. April 10 is the second-half date, with delinquency starting after May 10.

faqs.q: How much are late fees in Doña Ana County?
faqs.a: Each month adds 1% of the base tax in interest, and a 1% penalty builds for up to five months, with a $5 floor. Neither can be waived.

faqs.q: Can Doña Ana County property taxes be prorated?
faqs.a: No. Buyer and seller handle any sharing of the tax in their contract and at closing.

faqs.q: How long do I have to protest my Doña Ana County valuation?
faqs.a: Thirty days from the date on the Notice of Value, which typically falls in April. Later, a refund claim means paying in full and filing in District Court by January 10.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay Doña Ana County property tax?
faqs.a: On July 1, delinquent taxes are handed to the state Property Tax Division. Real property can then go to state auction after two unpaid years, or sooner with three or more years owing.
